source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals
finding: Founding paradigm. 428 online participants answered 8 CIA World Factbook percentage questions. They were then unexpectedly asked for a second, different guess, either at once or 3 weeks later. Neither group knew a second guess was coming, so they could not read it as a range. The average of the two guesses beat each single guess.
numbers: N=428 (immediate 255, delayed 173 by df). Original text: immediate, average beat guess 1 t(254)=2.25 p<.05 and guess 2 t(254)=6.08; delayed, t(172)=3.94 and 6.59. Second guesses were worse than first: t(254)=3.6, t(172)=2.8. Authors later said the true t values were larger (see Steegen 2014).
quote: averaging two guesses from one individual was more accurate than either guess alone
limits: Small short report, 8 items, one task type (percentage facts). Mean squared error is dominated by a few hard items.
agent_relevance: A model that resamples its own answer is the same design as asking a person twice: expect a gain even when the second sample is worse than the first.

source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals - size of the gain
finding: Gain from the inner crowd is small. Error cut relative to guess 1 was 2.5 to 10.4 percent (immediate) and 11.6 to 20.4 percent (delayed 3 weeks). Compared with asking another person, a second guess from yourself is worth about one tenth (immediate) or one third (delayed).
numbers: 95% CI of error reduced vs first guess: immediate [2.5%,10.4%], delayed [11.6%,20.4%]. Delay benefit larger: t(426)=2.12 p<.05 (corrected later to t=2.68, p=.008). Equivalent number of independent people: 1.11 (lambda=0.11) immediate, 1.32 (lambda=0.32) delayed.
quote: you can gain about 1/10th as much from asking yourself the same question twice as you can from getting a second opinion
limits: Equivalence comes from interpolating onto a fitted curve, so it is model dependent. Delay effect was not stable in the replication.
agent_relevance: Budget for 1.1 to 1.3 independent samples worth, not 2. More same-model samples have sharply diminishing value unless the samples are decorrelated.

source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals - formal model
finding: Formal model: across N different people, mean squared error of the average falls as a hyperbola toward the group bias, MSE(N)=a/N+b (fit R2=1). Within one person, N guesses reduce error by 1/[1+lambda(N-1)], where lambda is how much an extra guess from the same person is worth versus one from another person (0 = nothing, 1 = full).
numbers: Hyperbola fits across-person averages perfectly (R2=1). lambda=0.11 immediate, 0.32 delayed. Asymptote b = bias of the population belief, not of the person.
limits: The b term is shared bias, so no amount of averaging removes systematic error.
agent_relevance: Lets us predict the ceiling of resampling a single model: it converges to the model's own bias, and lambda measures how correlated its samples are.

source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals - theory
finding: Theory: a guess is a sample from an internal probability distribution, not a deterministic best guess. If so, two samples have partly independent noise and averaging cuts variance. If a guess were the single best estimate, a second guess would just add noise. Benefit despite worse second guesses supports sampling. A delay is said to reduce anchoring on the first guess.
numbers: Second guess less accurate than first in both conditions, yet average better than both. This rules out the account that people learned or looked up something between guesses.
limits: The paper does not separate sampling from other accounts, for example strategy change or memory retrieval noise. Prior work (Hirt and Markman 1995; Mussweiler et al. 2000) treated a second guess as a debiasing aid, not a sample.
agent_relevance: Matches how an LLM works: a decoder samples from a distribution, so the crowd-within idea is literally true for models at temperature above zero.

source: Ariely et al. (2000) The effects of averaging subjective probability estimates between and within judges (as described by Vul and Pashler 2008)
finding: Earlier test on probability judgments. Ariely and colleagues predicted a benefit from averaging probabilities within one judge but did not find it. Vul and Pashler explain why: probability judgments are biased toward 0 and 1, and averaging does not remove bias, only variance.
numbers: No numbers read this session (known only from Vul and Pashler's description).
limits: Second hand through Vul and Pashler (2008) and Fiechter and Kornell (2021). Boundary: the effect needs noise that is unbiased sampling around the truth.
agent_relevance: For probabilities or confidence output from a model, within-model averaging may give nothing when the model is systematically overconfident.

source: Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, Vanpaemel (2014) Measuring the crowd within again: a pre-registered replication study
finding: Pre-registered, high-powered replication at Leuven. Crowd within replicated in both the immediate and the 3-week delayed condition: the average beat guess 1 and guess 2 each time.
numbers: Immediate N=471: average MSE 541 vs guess 1 589 (t(470)=8.69, dz=0.40, CI [.31,.49]) and guess 2 615 (t=10.26, dz=0.47). Delayed N=140: average 467 vs guess 1 517 (t(139)=4.02, dz=0.34) and guess 2 589 (t=8.48, dz=0.72). Planned sample 439 immediate, 48 delayed. Second guess worse than first: dz -0.10 (immediate), -0.25 (delayed).
limits: Dutch student sample (mostly women, mean age 19.2 and 22.0) instead of an online pool; questions translated and answers updated. Delayed arm lost 91 of 231 people.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence the basic effect is real, with effect size dz about 0.3 to 0.5 against the first guess. It is real but modest.

source: Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, Vanpaemel (2014) Measuring the crowd within again: a pre-registered replication study - delay moderator
finding: The claim that a 3-week delay boosts the effect only half replicated. Versus guess 1 the delay gave no extra benefit; versus guess 2 it did (post hoc). In the original raw data the pattern was the reverse.
numbers: Gain vs guess 1: delayed 50 (SD 147) vs immediate 48 (SD 119), t(609)=0.18, p=.858, JZS Bayes factor 12.9 for no difference (reported in the table). Gain vs guess 2: delayed 121 vs immediate 73, t(609)=3.14, p=.002, d=0.30. In the original data the gain vs guess 2 difference was ns: t(426)=1.56, p=.12.
limits: Exploratory post hoc comparison; the authors say more work is needed. Different populations.
agent_relevance: Do not count on waiting or temporal separation as a reliable decorrelator. For a model there is no memory fade anyway; the analog is prompt variation, not delay.

source: Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, Vanpaemel (2014) Measuring the crowd within again: a pre-registered replication study - prior replication record and corrections
finding: Review of earlier attempts at the immediate condition: two supported it (Hourihan and Benjamin 2010; Rauhut and Lorenz 2011), Herzog and Hertwig 2009 found a gain whose interval included zero, and an unpublished attempt (Banker and McCoy) found a non-significant gain in the expected direction. The authors also learned that Vul and Pashler had under-reported their t values.
numbers: Herzog and Hertwig (as summarised in a footnote): median error gain 0.3 points (SD 2.3, Mdn 0%, CI [0.0, 0.8]), d=0.12. Banker and McCoy: MSE 463 to 452, n=201, t=2.15, dz=0.16 for guess 1. Pooled dz used for power: 0.17 vs guess 1, 0.56 vs guess 2. Corrected original t values: immediate 4.41 and 9.90, delayed 6.22 and 9.85.
limits: Early attempts used different accuracy measures (squared vs median absolute error), so effect sizes are not directly comparable. No delayed replication existed before this paper.
agent_relevance: Effect size against first guess is small (dz 0.12 to 0.40). A first-guess baseline is where the gain is smallest, and it is the honest comparison for a single-sample agent.

source: Hourihan and Benjamin (2010) Smaller is better (when sampling from the crowd within): low memory-span individuals benefit more from multiple opportunities for estimation
finding: Replicated Vul and Pashler with 170 students and found the gain larger for people with low working-memory span. Account: a smaller memory sample per guess overlaps less across guesses, so guesses are more independent.
numbers: N=170 after exclusions (181 recruited). Immediate replication MSE: average 484, guess 1 502 (t(169)=2.15, p=.03), guess 2 565 (t=7.89). Benefit vs OSPAN r=-.16, p<.05. Equivalent people: low span 1.07 (CI 1.05-1.09), high span 1.04 (CI 1.02-1.06). Median split: 86 low, 84 high.
limits: Span was measured not manipulated; group difference is tiny (1.07 vs 1.04); inference from CI overlap; only 8 items; 51 people got the second guess late in the session.
agent_relevance: Hint that the less a sampler draws from the same knowledge pool, the more independent its draws. Distinct retrieved evidence per sample could play that role.

source: Fiechter and Kornell (2021) How the wisdom of crowds, and of the crowd within, are affected by expertise
finding: Expertise boundary condition, tested with numerosity estimation (50-100 asterisks, 60 trials). Without training, both inner and outer crowd wisdom appear. After 12 practice trials with feedback, accuracy rose and variance collapsed; the inner crowd effect vanished while the outer crowd effect stayed.
numbers: Exp 1 N=63 (MTurk): hyperbola a/t+b; inner crowd a=0.05, b=0.09 (BF10 1417 for a); outer a=0.10, b=0.045. Exp 2 (trained): inner a=0.005 (SD .004, BF10 0.02, evidence for no effect), b=0.021; outer a=0.024, b=0.003.
limits: Numerosity is perceptual, not knowledge recall. Short training may overly constrain variance. Only two experiments.
agent_relevance: Warning: once a model is accurate and confident on an item, repeated samples are near-identical and averaging adds nothing. Gain concentrates on hard, high-variance items.

source: Fiechter and Kornell (2021) How the wisdom of crowds, and of the crowd within, are affected by expertise - diversity prediction theorem
finding: Formal frame: crowd wisdom (MSE minus bias) equals the variance of the estimates (Page's diversity prediction theorem). So any inner-crowd gain is capped by response variance, and a method that lowers variance by making answers more correct also removes the gain. Delay helps, on this account, because it lowers correlation between samples.
numbers: Worked example in paper: crowd A MSE 116.33, bias 0.11, variance 116.22; crowd B MSE 1.67, bias 0.11, variance 1.56. Wisdom = variance.
limits: A tautology of squared error, so it describes but does not explain why variance arises.
agent_relevance: Gives a quick diagnostic: measure variance across resamples. If it is near zero, resampling is wasted compute.

source: Fiechter and Kornell (2021) How the wisdom of crowds, and of the crowd within, are affected by expertise - literature list of settings
finding: Lists where the inner crowd has been observed: percentage estimation, numerical knowledge estimation, date estimation, quantity estimation (counting objects, natural experiment). Delay benefit said to replicate in Steegen 2014 and van Dolder and van den Assem 2018. Notes a mixed record for numerical general-knowledge items (Rauhut and Lorenz found it; Muller-Trede did not, per the 'but see').
numbers: Cites: Fraundorf and Benjamin 2014, Herzog and Hertwig 2009, Hourihan and Benjamin 2010, Muller-Trede 2011, Rauhut and Lorenz 2011, Steegen 2014, van Dolder and van den Assem 2018.
limits: Second hand for the cited studies. The statement that delay replicated contrasts with Steegen's own mixed result.
agent_relevance: Effect is task dependent. Check it on our own task type before assuming a gain.

source: Herzog and Hertwig (2009) The wisdom of many in one mind: improving individual judgments with dialectical bootstrapping (as described in Gomilsek et al. 2024 and Steegen 2014)
finding: Dialectical bootstrapping. Participants estimated years of historical events, then were told to assume the first estimate was wrong, think of reasons why, and give a second estimate. Averaging the pair beat the first estimate and beat a control with no strategy. Named after Hegel (thesis, antithesis, synthesis).
numbers: Control (no strategy) in the 2009 data: median error gain 0.3 points (SD 2.3), CI [0.0, 0.8], d=0.12 (Steegen footnote). Dialectical figures not read this session; full paper paywalled.
limits: Second hand. The second estimate was made with the first shown, so strategy and memory aid were confounded (see Gomilsek 2024). 20 percent trimmed averages were used.
agent_relevance: Closest human analogue to a prompt that says: assume your answer is wrong and give another. Gain depends on the opposite being a genuine new view, not noise.

source: Gomilsek et al. (2024) Fermian guesstimation can boost the wisdom-of-the-inner-crowd
finding: Tested dialectical bootstrapping (consider-the-opposite) against a Fermi-style strategy (decompose and aggregate sub-estimates) and a control, crossed with showing or hiding the first estimate. Animal-property estimates (body weight, brain weight, lifespan, gestation, sleep). Fermian strategy gave the largest untrimmed error reduction, but the ranking flipped with 20 percent participant-trimming.
numbers: N=285 Prolific (292 recruited). 40 items per person used (50 collected, body weight dropped). Untrimmed mean error reduction: Fermian aided 2.6% (d=0.34, p=.013), unaided 3.9% (d=0.31, p=.017). Trimmed: dialectical 1.55% (aided, p=.086, d=0.25) and 1.35% (unaided, p=.026, d=0.36); Fermian 0.34% and 1.02%. Helpful bracketing 9.3, 5.1, 4.7, 13.9, 10.2, 9.0 percent across six conditions; unhelpful 4.1, 1.8, 2.5, 5.6, 3.9, 3.4.
limits: Result depends on trimming rule (a reanalysis dispute with White and Antonakis 2013). Effects are 1 to 4 percent error reduction. Software error forced dropping body-weight items.
agent_relevance: Decomposition (Fermi) as a second-sample generator fits our schema idea of structured alternatives, with small gains. Report results under several outlier rules.

source: Gomilsek et al. (2024) Fermian guesstimation can boost the wisdom-of-the-inner-crowd - versus asking someone else
finding: Asking oneself again lost to asking another person in every condition: averaging your first estimate with another participant's first estimate was closer to the truth more often than averaging with your own second one.
numbers: In all 6 conditions asking someone else was better more often; mean superiority 8.3 percentage points (SE 0.8). Smallest in the two Fermian conditions. Participants believed 61.7% of true values were in their 90% ranges (SD 22.4) - overprecision. Fermian reduced overprecision slightly (1.7 and 0.9 points).
limits: Within-experiment comparison only, one task.
agent_relevance: Cross-model or cross-prompt diversity should beat same-model resampling, which fits the correlated-error results in the LLM section.

source: Gomilsek et al. (2024) Fermian guesstimation can boost the wisdom-of-the-inner-crowd - review of weaknesses and debate
finding: Records the dispute: White and Antonakis (2013) reanalysed Herzog and Hertwig's data, did not exactly reproduce the dialectical gain, and drew different conclusions with four other accuracy measures. Possible cause: 20 percent trimmed participant averages. Follow-up studies of dialectical bootstrapping found success in some task types and failure in others.
numbers: No new numbers; describes H&H as 20 percent trimming (middle 60 percent of participants).
limits: Second hand for the White and Antonakis paper (not opened).
agent_relevance: Treat any reported gain from a reconsider-your-answer step as fragile until checked with untrimmed, item-level metrics.

source: Fraundorf and Benjamin (2014) Knowing the crowd within: metacognitive limits on combining multiple judgments
finding: People do not know when to average. After two estimates, participants chose first, second or the average. They averaged on 43 to 59 percent of items, but choosing was no better than chance with item-specific numbers only. Showing general labels plus numbers gave modest trial-by-trial selection. Always averaging beat their chosen values.
numbers: Pooled N about 212. Pooled MSE: first 537, second 606, average 500 (average vs first t(212)=4.27, p<.001). Study 1A labels only N=61: averaged 59%, MSE actual 561 vs always-average 541 (p<.05). Study 1B numbers only N=51: averaged 43%, choosing accuracy 47%, preferred the worse second estimate. Study 3 N=54: combined cues, choosing accuracy 56%; break-even required 67%; only 17 of 52 reached it.
limits: 12 percentage questions; one pooled N inconsistency; Study 2 underpowered; recency/fluency explanation not directly tested.
agent_relevance: Never let the agent choose between its samples on gut feel. A fixed rule (always average or vote) beats self-selection unless the selector is better than about 2 in 3.

source: Rauhut and Lorenz (2011) The wisdom of crowds in one mind (as described in Steegen 2014, Fiechter and Kornell 2021 and Fujisaki et al. 2025)
finding: Participants gave several estimates (five, per Fujisaki 2025) to numerical questions. Per the later papers, averaging own estimates helped a little, but accuracy did not keep improving as the number of own estimates grew, unlike pooling different people. Fiechter and Kornell adopted its a/t+b curve fit.
numbers: Not read this session; second-hand summary only. Fujisaki 2025 says in the repeated condition the MSE stayed flat from one to five estimates, and credits Rauhut and Lorenz with the point that more own estimates do not help much.
limits: Second hand. Steegen could not use its data because the paper did not report enough for effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Plan for sharp saturation: the 2nd to 5th sample from the same model adds little.

source: van Dolder and van den Assem (2018) The wisdom of the inner crowd in three large natural experiments (as cited in Fiechter and Kornell 2021)
finding: Three large field datasets of repeated guesses (quantity estimation, per Fiechter and Kornell: guessing the number of objects). Observational, not lab. Described as showing the inner crowd effect and the benefit of time between guesses. Article paywalled; not opened.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second hand only; observational, so people chose whether to re-guess.
agent_relevance: Large-sample evidence outside the lab that the small positive effect is real.

source: Page diversity prediction theorem as used by Fujisaki et al. (2025)
finding: Fujisaki et al. use the decomposition: collective error = average individual squared error minus diversity (variance around the mean). They show their multi-perspective method has worse individual accuracy but more diversity, and diversity wins.
numbers: Ensemble method had higher expected squared error than repeated estimates but lower collective error, because diversity was larger.
limits: Describes, does not create diversity.
agent_relevance: Score samples on both accuracy and diversity; selecting samples only for individual accuracy kills the gain.

source: Van de Calseyde and Efendic (2025) Disagreeing perspectives enhance inner-crowd wisdom for difficult (but not easy) questions
finding: Three pre-registered experiments (N=2,884) reconcile a dispute. Taking a disagreeing perspective for the second guess raised bracketing and diversity. Overall benefit was mixed after a maximal random-effects reanalysis (Fiechter). The effect depends on question difficulty: helps on hard questions, hurts on easy ones.
numbers: Exp 1a N=1,193, Exp 1b N=1,196, Exp 2 N=501 (Prolific, US/UK). Exp 2 interaction of difficulty and perspective: estimate -13.49, error 3.15, 95% CrI [-19.77, -7.34]; averaging benefit with disagreeing perspective 18.75. Bracketing in Exp 2: 22% self-perspective vs 35% disagreeing. Exp 1a overall: -19.31, CrI [-51.90, 13.09] (no benefit; average benefit 76.8 disagreeing vs 56.6 self). 120 items ranked by first-guess MSE.
limits: Difficulty is defined by crowd error on first guesses, which is partly circular. Two guesses only.
agent_relevance: Forced diversity helps only where the first answer is far off. A router that detects item difficulty (disagreement across samples) should decide when to add perspectives.

source: Fujisaki, Yang, Ueda (2023) On an effective and efficient method for exploiting the wisdom of the inner crowd
finding: Other-perspective method: give your own estimate, then estimate what people in general would say, and average. It beat dialectical bootstrapping and plain repeated guesses on MSE reduction and took less time than dialectical. People using the method also improved their final self-chosen answer.
numbers: Exp 1 N=452 Japanese adults, 3 conditions: MSE-reduction 95% CIs: Other's perspective [29.40,75.63], Dialectical [19.69,68.92], Repeated [-1.46,33.70]. Exp 2 (lab): Other [57.66,136.18], Dialectical [-5.57,51.47], Repeated [20.00,63.72]; Other beat Dialectical t(82)=3.23 p=.005. Final estimate better than first only in Other (t(1072)=2.20, p=.028). Exp 3 (4 public-opinion estimates): no gain over one (t(57)=0.032, p=.97), because the estimates were too similar.
limits: Gains larger when the person is confident in the first estimate (F(1,531.6)=10.30, p=.0014). In Exp 1 the Other vs Dialectical difference was ns (p=.81).
agent_relevance: A persona prompt (what would others say) is cheap and may decorrelate more than repeated sampling; but repeating the same persona saturates after one.

source: Fujisaki et al. (2025) An ensemble method utilising multiple thinking styles that boosts the wisdom-of-inner-crowd effect
finding: Combining five different thinking styles (intuition, deliberation, dialectic, general-crowd view, disagreeing-other view) gave an inner crowd whose error kept falling with more estimates, while five plain repeated estimates stayed flat. Still worth only about 1.5 people, below two independent people even at infinite estimates.
numbers: Experiment N=64 students; Ensemble MSE vs 5 repeated estimates t=2.51, p=.012, d=0.59; vs repeated first estimate t=2.19, p=.029; Page trend z=-5.15 (ensemble) vs z=1.09, p=.28 (repeated). Equivalent persons at 5 estimates 1.51. Pilot: Intuition vs Deliberation average d=0.35, p=.054. Prior claim in the paper: inner crowd average worth 1.1 to 1.4 persons.
limits: Small N, fixed order of styles, no accuracy incentives, percentage questions only; ensemble first estimate alone is worse than control.
agent_relevance: Support for heterogeneous prompts (different reasoning styles) rather than temperature resampling, with a firm ceiling about 2 independent samples.

source: Authors not recorded (2026) Two out of three ain't bad: aggregating multiple identification decisions from the same observer improves unfamiliar face matching
finding: Crowd within in a perceptual decision task (unfamiliar face matching, 80 trials). Aggregating the same person's 2 or 3 responses raised accuracy; aggregating different people raised it more. A week's delay did not increase the effect.
numbers: Exp 1 N=125 (Prolific, 3 blocks in one session); Exp 2 final N=83, weekly blocks. Exp 2: AUC gain 5.9 percent after block 2 and 7.9 percent after block 3 (overall accuracy +2.3% and +4.8%). Prior work cited: AUC about 5% after two decisions. Block 1 accuracy 80.0 (SD 9.5) Exp 2 vs 81.8 (SD 7.8) Exp 1.
limits: Perceptual rather than knowledge task; Prolific samples; gain larger for match than mismatch trials.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect extends to repeated classification judgments, not just numeric estimates, but still below the cross-person gain.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Sampling many reasoning chains from one model and taking a majority vote on the final answer is a crowd within for LLMs. Large gains on arithmetic and commonsense reasoning over greedy chain-of-thought.
numbers: GSM8K +17.9 (PaLM-540B 56.5 to 74.4; Codex-002 60.1 to 78.0), SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9. LaMDA-137B GSM8K 17.1 to 27.7; UL2-20B 4.1 to 7.3. 40 sampled paths; T=0.5 (UL2, LaMDA) and 0.7 (PaLM), top-k 40. Gains of +3 to 6 for UL2-20B, +9 to 23 for LaMDA-137B.
limits: Majority vote suits tasks with a single discrete answer. Gains smaller on tasks near ceiling (PaLM-540B AddSub +1.8). Sample count and temperature matter; heavy compute.
agent_relevance: The main LLM evidence that same-model resampling pays: large on mid-difficulty math chains. Voting, not averaging free text.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need
finding: Sampling and voting with more copies of the same LLM ('Agent Forest') keeps improving accuracy with ensemble size, and the gain is larger for harder tasks. Small models can match bigger ones.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama2-13B with ensemble reaches 59% vs Llama2-70B single 54%; ensemble 15 matches Llama2-70B, ensemble 15 and 20 bring Llama2-70B and GPT-3.5-Turbo to par. HumanEval gains 4 to 9 percent. Works on top of SPP, CoT and other methods (e.g. Llama2-70B SPP GSM8K 0.42 to 0.69).
limits: Gain correlates with task difficulty; diminishing returns; extra inference cost; vote needs comparable answers.
agent_relevance: Confirms ensembles scale with count for same-model sampling; budget N by item difficulty.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: LLM analogue of dialectical bootstrapping (ask the model to reconsider with no external feedback) did not help and often hurt, while plain self-consistency at equal cost did. Reported benefits came from oracle labels. Multi-agent debate was no better than self-consistency at equal responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 baseline. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. Self-consistency GSM8K: 1 response 76.7, 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; prompts taken from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence that a second look ('assume you were wrong') is not a free dialectical gain; independent resample-and-vote is the reliable form.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
finding: Averaging forecasts across 12 different LLMs matched a human crowd on 31 binary Metaculus questions. This is a between-model crowd, not an inner crowd; each model was queried three times. Showing the human median to the model improved its forecast.
numbers: Median LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=.85. 1007 forecasts. ANOVA across models F(12,354)=2.64, p=.002. Study 2: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 after seeing human median (p=.003). Acquiescence bias, mean forecast 57.35 (SD 20.93), overconfidence.
limits: Only 31 questions over 3 months; individual models weaker than the aggregate; models show acquiescence bias that averaging cannot fix.
agent_relevance: Mixing different models gives the cross-person crowd that the inner crowd lacks. Averaging cannot remove shared bias.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models
finding: LLM errors are strongly correlated: when two models are both wrong they agree about 60 percent of the time. More accurate and larger models are more correlated, even across providers. This sets the ceiling for ensembles, and same-model resampling is likely more correlated still.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HuggingFace leaderboard); 71 LLMs on 14,042 (HELM); 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. Agreement when both wrong about 60% (random chance 1/3). Same provider, same architecture and similar size raise correlation.
limits: Multiple-choice items mostly; a model's correlation with itself under sampling is not the subject (that last point is our inference).
agent_relevance: Direct support for the low-lambda prediction: model copies share errors, so expect gains below the human inner crowd and capped by shared bias.
